title: The consequences of the US midterm elections
gist: Five IISS senior fellows assess the 3 November 2026 midterms, in which Democrats won both chambers (possibly 56 Senate seats) amid anger over corruption, cost of living and the Iran war. They expect aggressive oversight and contract scrutiny, AI data-centre headwinds, stalled defence budgets/NDAA and pressure on defence-tech start-ups, while Trump's lame-duck foreign policy stays unchanged or becomes more impulsive.

themes.theme: Democratic sweep and new congressional leverage (2027-29)

insights.claim: In the 3 November 2026 US midterms Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and may hold as many as 56 of 100 Senate seats, including traditional GOP strongholds Texas and Kansas, despite having only an estimated one-in-three chance of winning the Senate in early 2026.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Scale of the upset implies markets/pollsters badly underpriced political regime change; reprice policy-risk assumptions for 2027-28.
insights.quote: the party may start the next congress controlling as many as 56 seats out of 100
insights.locator: Fraioli: In winning control of both chambers

insights.claim: Exit polls showed voters rated government corruption (55%), the high cost of living (49%) and the war against Iran (34%) as 'crucial' issues in the 2026 midterms.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Corruption and affordability, not just war, drove the vote; expect Democratic agenda to target these themes.
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands

insights.claim: From 3 January 2027 to January 2029 congressional Democrats can use federal funding deadlines to extract concessions from the White House and can investigate both the administration and companies that dealt closely with it since 2025.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Funding-deadline brinkmanship and probes become recurring event risks for 2027-28.
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands

insights.claim: Companies with federal contracts or deals negotiated under Trump should expect closer scrutiny of how those arrangements were made, and firms that relied on personal ties to the White House must now manage relations with congressional Democrats.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Headline/regulatory risk for 'Trump-connected' contractors; relationship-based moats erode.
insights.quote: Those with federal contracts or deals negotiated under Trump should expect closer scrutiny
insights.locator: Fraioli: From 3 January 2027

insights.claim: A Democratic-controlled Senate can reject Trump's judicial and senior-executive nominees, meaning even a replacement for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, if he resigned or were removed, would face an unclear confirmation path.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Expect acting officials and personnel paralysis across agencies; policy execution slows.
insights.locator: Caverley: Lame-duck militarism or aggressive oversight?

insights.claim: Before the new Congress convenes, Trump can press the outgoing Senate to confirm judges and may support or file lawsuits in close races and launch further voter-fraud prosecutions.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Lame-duck window (Nov 2026-Jan 2027) carries elevated institutional/legal noise.
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands

themes.theme: AI and data-centre backlash as a political force

insights.claim: Texas, previously a development-friendly jurisdiction for AI data centres, elected a Democratic governor who campaigned on a data-centre moratorium.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Siting/permitting risk rises in a key data-centre hub; watch Texas policy on power and land for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: elected a Democratic Party governor who campaigned on a data-centre moratorium
insights.locator: Fraioli: The artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre build-out

insights.claim: Voters chose to limit or restrict data-centre development in nearly all of approximately 41 related ballot measures across the US in the 2026 midterms.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Local opposition is broad-based, not isolated; build-out timelines and capex plans face state/local headwinds.
insights.quote: Voters chose to limit or restrict data-centre development in nearly all of the approximately 41 related ballot measures nationwide
insights.locator: Fraioli: The artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre build-out

insights.claim: Democrats believe their AI- and data-centre-sceptical stance contributed to their win, signalling they will carry it into 2028, which has lowered investor expectations for AI capital investment in a sector already facing correction risk.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: AI capex consensus faces a political discount; anti-data-centre positioning likely a 2028 platform plank.
insights.quote: which has lowered future expectations among investors regarding AI capital investment in a sector already facing correction risk
insights.locator: Fraioli: The artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre build-out

insights.claim: During the campaign Trump responded to widespread voter concern about AI by declaring that anyone who did not call it 'superior intelligence' was 'the enemy', illustrating a pro-AI stance at odds with public sentiment.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Partisan polarisation of AI raises odds AI policy swings with party control.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: The pace of artificial-intelligence development could produce turmoil over the rest of the decade rivalling or exceeding the events that brought down the Carter presidency, complicating any projected Democratic ascendancy.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Treat AI disruption as a macro-political shock variable for 2028 and beyond.
insights.locator: Allin: Earthquake

themes.theme: Iran war, energy prices and the electoral cost of foreign policy

insights.claim: The Iran war's main electoral pain point was soaring gasoline and diesel prices, showing foreign and domestic policy are intertwined, though polls showed the war was hugely unpopular even before economic effects hit.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Energy prices are the transmission mechanism from geopolitics to US elections; watch fuel prices as a political indicator.
insights.locator: Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: In one nationally representative poll, 63% said the US made the 'wrong decision on Iran' and 74% said the conflict was a 'crucial' or 'major' factor in their vote.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Strong public mandate against escalation constrains Iran policy.
insights.locator: Caverley: Lame-duck militarism or aggressive oversight?

insights.claim: Contrary to the view that the 2026 midterms were a foreign-policy election, an AP poll found 40% named the economy and 30% the state of democracy as their top issue, with very few choosing foreign policy; the war's effect was mostly indirect via prices.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Democrats will frame security policy through cost-of-living and democracy lenses.
insights.locator: Caverley: Lame-duck militarism or aggressive oversight?

insights.claim: The 2026 result corrects the commonplace idea that foreign policy is negligible in US elections: the Iran war, tariffs against allies, mass-deportation policy and the 'imperial presidency' all played a huge role.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Contrasts with other IISS view; signals disagreement on how much foreign policy drove the vote.
insights.quote: a corrective to the commonplace idea that foreign policy plays a negligible role in American electoral politics
insights.locator: Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: Despite Trump raising prospects of post-midterm escalation against Iran, the scale of the Democratic victory and ongoing Israeli coalition negotiations make escalation less likely, and the surviving Republican caucus would prefer lower energy prices.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Reduced escalation odds argue for easing energy risk premium; monitor Israeli coalition outcome.
insights.quote: the surviving Republican caucus would no doubt prefer lower energy prices
insights.locator: Caverley: Iran and Ukraine

insights.claim: Rather than ending the Iran conflict that was the primary cause of higher energy prices, Trump brokered an ineffectual diesel deal with Russia while trying to scapegoat Zelenskyy for continuing the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Signals preference for transactional Russia deals over resolving the energy shock's root cause.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: Vice President JD Vance wrote that 'the reason we lost is the war', and posted a list of defeat reasons starting with the Iran war and ending with America's relationship with Israel.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Vance positioning signals a restraint/anti-interventionist lane in the GOP 2028 contest, with implications for Israel policy.
insights.quote: ‘the reason we lost is the war’
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands

themes.theme: Lame-duck Trump: foreign policy as the unconstrained arena

insights.claim: With his domestic agenda blocked, Trump will probably turn further toward foreign policy, imposing his vision on international economic and alliance issues even more, plus personal-imprint projects like Washington DC construction.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Expect more trade/alliance volatility, not less, through January 2029.
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands

insights.claim: Lame-duck presidents with a stymied domestic agenda historically become more active in foreign policy in their final years.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Base rate supports higher foreign-policy event risk in 2027-28.
insights.locator: Caverley: Lame-duck militarism or aggressive oversight?

insights.claim: Electoral defeat is more likely to make Trump's foreign policy more impulsive than moderate it, since he faces no further elections and fewer constraints abroad.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Don't price a moderation trade; tail risks in tariffs and alliances persist.
insights.quote: this electoral defeat does not moderate Trump’s foreign policy, but in fact makes it more impulsive
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: At least in the short term, the guiding coordinates of Trumpian foreign policy—hostility to liberal European governments, casting Zelenskyy as a Democratic ally, and viewing Putin and Xi as dealmaking partners—will remain unchanged because Trump, at 80, is unlikely to change his worldview.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Congressional shift doesn't change the executive's foreign-policy direction; NATO/Europe risk unchanged.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: Since December 2025, encouraging the replacement of liberal European governments with far-right alternatives has been the Trump administration's stated policy.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Ongoing US interference risk in European politics; transatlantic friction persists.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: A scenario in which around a dozen Republican senators join Democrats to threaten Trump with conviction unless he moderates remains highly unlikely, and Democrats have limited appetite for another impeachment attempt after two failures.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Removal risk is negligible; investigations, not impeachment, are the main lever.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy / Stevenson: Can the Democrats restrain President Trump?

insights.claim: Whether the US honours NATO commitments remains Trump's decision until January 2029, and a Democratic Congress is unlikely to make him respond more firmly to a Russian incursion into NATO territory.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: European defence self-reliance demand stays elevated regardless of midterm result.
insights.locator: Rhode: Key coordinates of foreign policy

insights.claim: Trump's opponents envision ever-higher tariffs, Iran escalation, harsher immigration enforcement and further hobbling of Ukraine in favour of lucrative deals with Russia, since Trump appears to take the defeat personally.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Tariff and sanctions-relief risks remain live under a lame-duck president.
insights.locator: Stevenson: Can the Democrats restrain President Trump?

themes.theme: Defence budget, NDAA and defence-tech pressure

insights.claim: The Trump administration requested US$1.5 trillion in defence spending in April 2026, excluding Iran-war costs, but the House has not voted on the defence appropriations bill and the Senate version has not left committee; industry accepts a Democratic legislature is even less likely to fund that top line.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Defence top-line expectations should be cut; primes' budget-growth assumptions at risk.
insights.locator: Caverley: Defence budgeting and authorisation

insights.claim: The federal continuing resolution expires on 11 December 2026; another continuing resolution until the new Congress is sworn in is most likely, with a full government shutdown as the worst case.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Near-term fiscal event risk; CRs delay new defence program starts.
insights.locator: Caverley: Defence budgeting and authorisation

insights.claim: The 2027 NDAA is uncertain despite 65 consecutive years of passage, because parties are deadlocked over whether the Iran war can continue without formal congressional authorisation, and Trump could veto a bill adding that requirement.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: A first NDAA failure in 65 years would disrupt Pentagon programs; watch war-authorisation fight.
insights.quote: Congress has passed a National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) each of the past 65 years
insights.locator: Caverley: More unusually, and perhaps more consequentially

insights.claim: Regardless of party control, US defence acquisition will focus on rebuilding severely depleted munitions stocks, which alone exceeds current defence-industrial-base capacity, so any new US support for Ukraine will be modest.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Munitions makers have durable demand; Ukraine aid upside limited.
insights.quote: that alone is currently more than the US defence-industrial base can handle
insights.locator: Caverley: Iran and Ukraine

insights.claim: A Democratic Congress is unlikely to bring Ukraine much relief because Trump has waived most of the Russia sanctions required by the 2026 Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
insights.speaker: IISS
entities: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act
insights.so_what: Russia sanctions relief via executive waiver persists despite Congress.
insights.locator: Caverley: Iran and Ukraine

insights.claim: Greater oversight of opaquely awarded contracts to new defence-acquisition entrants (rare earths to uncrewed systems), plus recognition that procurement dollars won't deliver venture-capital-level returns, is likely to pressure the many American defence-tech start-ups.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for VC-backed defence tech valuations and contract-dependent new entrants.
insights.quote: is likely to put pressure on the large numbers of American defence tech start-ups
insights.locator: Caverley: Given that Elon Musk spent

insights.claim: There is partisan and national-security logic to investigating Elon Musk, given he spent over half a billion dollars backing Republican midterm candidates, led the Department of Government Efficiency, and Starlink access for Ukrainian forces was recently throttled.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Musk-linked firms (SpaceX/Starlink) face congressional probe and contract-scrutiny risk.
insights.quote: Elon Musk spent over half a billion dollars in support of Republican midterm candidates
insights.locator: Caverley: Given that Elon Musk spent

insights.claim: Incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia responded to the Democratic wave with a two-word post, 'lawyer up', signalling aggressive use of subpoenas and hearings.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Expect a heavy subpoena calendar hitting administration figures and connected firms.
insights.locator: Caverley: Oversight

insights.claim: The 2026 midterms were the biggest opposition landslide since the 1974 post-Watergate election, but 1974 counsels caution about projecting a lasting Democratic ascendancy: Carter's presidency became 'a parenthesis inside 20 years of Republican presidents'.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: A wave election doesn't guarantee durable control; don't over-extrapolate 2028.
insights.quote: ‘the Carter administration turned out to be a parenthesis inside 20 years of Republican presidents’
insights.locator: Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: Unlike Nixon, who arguably left the US in a stronger strategic position and had a concept of the West to defend, Trump lacks that strategic acumen, and there is no Republican equivalent of the neoconservative defence intellectuals who powered Reaganism.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: GOP foreign-policy realignment after Trump is ideologically unanchored; restraint vs hawk fight unresolved.
insights.locator: Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: The Republican succession contest will intensify over the next six months, but JD Vance faces a bind running on a right-wing 'Come Home, America' platform while avoiding a damaging break with Trump.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Watch Vance's distancing from Iran war/Israel policy as a GOP direction signal.
insights.locator: Fraioli: Congress changes hands / Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: Democrats flipped traditionally Republican states largely through disciplined centrist campaigns, and prominent progressives such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have become more pragmatic, suggesting greater party cohesion into 2028.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: A centrist, cohesive Democratic party lowers left-tail policy risk in 2028 pricing.
insights.locator: Stevenson: Can the Democrats restrain President Trump?

insights.claim: To sustain momentum into 2028, Democrats must prioritise the cost of living, damage to democracy and unnecessary military intervention, while managing a vast gap between expectations and limited power under Trump.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Affordability-focused legislation/messaging likely dominates 2027-28 agenda.
insights.locator: Stevenson: Can the Democrats restrain President Trump? / Allin: Earthquake

insights.claim: The midterm disaster will conclusively sour some Republicans on Trumpism, which may non-trivially raise bipartisan willingness to constrain the president, while the Supreme Court will likely take note of the political tide.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Incremental institutional checks on executive action could rise; watch court rulings on executive power.
insights.locator: Stevenson: Can the Democrats restrain President Trump?
